title: L’Anse aux Meadows: a date for an activity
intro: A precise date can transform a discussion without answering every question about a settlement.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.text: Kuitems and colleagues used the radiocarbon signal associated with AD 993 and tree-ring measurements to date Norse activity at the Newfoundland site to AD 1021.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.text: The study supplies a firm chronological point within the history of Norse activity in the Americas. Read it alongside the archaeological site record.

sections.heading: What remains open
sections.text: This date alone does not establish first arrival, the total length of occupation, or which named saga traveller was present. Those are separate historical questions.

title: Birka Bj.581: burial, biology and interpretation
intro: The strongest conclusions are clearer when biological analysis and social interpretation are kept distinct.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.text: The 2019 reassessment discusses a richly furnished weapon burial whose skeletal and genomic analysis identified the buried individual as biologically female.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.text: Price and colleagues argue for a professional warrior identity. Their article examines the grave’s context and responds to debate following the 2017 genetic publication.

sections.heading: What remains open
sections.text: Biological sex does not by itself reveal an occupation or a person’s self-understanding. The meaning of the burial assemblage requires interpretation, and one burial cannot establish how common any role was.

title: Gjellestad: from radar trace to investigation
period: Early Viking Age, as reported in 2020
intro: A case study in how one kind of investigation leads to another.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.text: NIKU reports that ground-penetrating radar detected the ship in 2018. Its January 2020 update describes preliminary investigation and timber dating supporting an early Viking Age attribution.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.text: The agreement between survey results and later investigation supports the identification of an archaeological ship. The report connects its setting with burial mounds and buildings.

sections.heading: What remains open
sections.text: Radar shapes do not provide a complete biography of a site. This entry covers the 2018–2020 milestone and does not present it as the project’s latest excavation report.

title: The Galloway Hoard: objects and their wrapping
intro: The materials around an object can be evidence in their own right.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.text: National Museums Scotland describes a hoard discovered in 2014, buried around AD 900, with precious objects and surviving textiles and leather around them.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.text: Studying those materials can help researchers investigate how objects were gathered and prepared for burial. The museum places the work within a wider study of Viking Age hoarding.

sections.heading: What remains open
sections.text: A hoard is not a transparent label for its owner’s identity. The makers, users and people who buried its objects may have been different; the reason for burial requires an argument.

title: Skuldelev: ships made into a barrier
intro: A vessel’s final use may be very different from the purpose for which it was built.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.text: The Viking Ship Museum describes five deliberately sunk ships forming a barrier in Roskilde Fjord. Its account dates the first phase to about 1060–1070 and records excavation in 1962.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.text: The museum suggests protection from seaborne attack or control of traffic as possible purposes. Its reconstructions draw on documented surviving parts.

sections.heading: What remains open
sections.text: Missing and deformed timbers make reconstruction an interpretive process. A reconstructed vessel should be distinguished from the archaeological remains on which it is based.
